header.source: KNOWLEDGE · etymology joined to atoms, anon door

rows.definition: The rearranging of a whole's parts and their relations. Restructuring changes what is possible without changing what is there.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A change made to how the house's own parts relate to one another, done without discarding what already stood — what becomes possible changes, not what is there.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin structura (a building, a fitting together), from struere (to pile up, build), with re- (again) prefixed; a rearranging of what was already built rather than a building from nothing.

rows.definition: What comes back after a thing is done. From the Latin for rebound - a result is the leap returning, not the leap.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: What comes back once a process has run its course — an outcome standing apart from the steps that produced it, ready to be read on its own.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin resultare (to spring back, rebound), a frequentative of resilire (re- back + salire, to leap); the outcome named as a rebound from an action rather than the action itself.

rows.definition: To take up again what was paused. Resuming assumes the state was kept.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Picking a paused thing back up from exactly where it stood, trusting that its state was kept rather than lost.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin resumere (to take up again), from re- (again) + sumere (to take, assume); picking up a suspended action rather than beginning it anew.

rows.definition: How long a thing is kept before it is let go. A retention rule is an ethical decision wearing a technical name.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: How long a kept thing is allowed to stay before it must be released — a boundary decided in advance rather than discovered by accident.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin retinere (to hold back, keep), from re- (back) + tenere (to hold); retention names the choice to keep holding a thing rather than let it go.

rows.definition: To draw back what was extended — a claim withdrawn, a reach returned; reversal done openly.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Drawing back a claim or a reach that went too far, done openly rather than left to quietly lapse.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin retrahere (to draw back), from re- (back) + trahere (to draw, pull); a withdrawal made by the same hand that made the original reach.

rows.definition: To draw back to safer ground — withdrawal as wisdom, not defeat; and the quiet place one withdraws to.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A step back taken on purpose, and the quiet place that step leads to — withdrawal read as care for what continues, not as loss.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French retraite (a drawing back), from Latin retrahere (to draw back) — the same root as retract, but kept for a deliberate, safer withdrawal rather than an undoing.

rows.definition: The bringing back of what was stored. Retrieval is the whole reason keeping is done at all.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The bringing back of what was stored — the one part of keeping that ever gets tested, since a keeping nobody can retrieve was never really kept.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French retrouver (to find again), from re- (again) + trouver (to find); retrieval assumes something once had and since set aside is being found, not made.

rows.definition: To bring back what was stored. Retrieval assumes the keeping was done well enough to find it again.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The act of finding again what was set aside — the moment a kept thing proves it was kept well.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French retrouver (to find again), from re- (again) + trouver (to find); the verb names the act of finding, not merely the fact of it.

rows.definition: To attempt again after failing. Retrying assumes the failure was of the moment rather than of the method.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A second attempt made in good faith, on the wager that what failed was the moment and not the method.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French trier (to sift, pick out, examine), of uncertain further origin, prefixed with re- (again); a second sifting, on the chance the first pass merely misfired.

rows.definition: To come back, and to give back. Both senses close a circuit that was opened.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Both a coming back and a giving back — the closing of a circuit that was deliberately left open, whichever direction the closing runs.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French retorner (to turn back), from re- (again) + torner (to turn), from Latin tornare (to turn on a lathe); a circuit that closes, whether of a body coming back or a thing given back.

rows.definition: To look again at a thing with judgment. A review is a second seeing, made deliberately.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A second seeing done deliberately, with judgment attached — the look a thing gets after the first look is already finished.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin re- (again) + videre (to see), via Old French reveoir; a review is literally a second seeing, undertaken on purpose rather than by accident.

rows.definition: To see again and amend — change made by second sight, in the open.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Changing something because it was looked at again and seen differently — amendment made in the open, by the same second sight the word names.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin revisere (to visit again, look at again), from re- (again) + visere (to go see), a frequentative of videre (to see); amendment made by that second sight rather than by guesswork.

rows.definition: What good doing brings back — return earned, not extracted; in this house's games, the reward is the words.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: What good doing brings back, and in this house's games that return is never taken from anyone else — the words themselves are the whole of it.
rows.historical_meaning: Old North French rewarder (to look back at, take heed of), a doublet of regard, from re- (back) + warder (to watch, guard), of Germanic origin; a reward was first the attention paid back for what someone had done.

rows.definition: Colour stated as amounts of red, green and blue. A named encoding rather than a concept.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Colour stated as three measured amounts rather than as a single word — precise enough for a machine to reproduce exactly.
rows.historical_meaning: An initialism formed from the English words red, green and blue, fixed by twentieth-century colour science and display technology rather than descended from an older word.

rows.definition: Colour stated as red, green, blue and how opaque it is. A named encoding rather than a concept.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The rgb encoding with one more number added for how see-through a colour is — opacity stated as plainly as the colour itself.
rows.historical_meaning: An initialism extending rgb with alpha, the letter conventionally used in computing for a transparency value; a modern coinage rather than an inherited word.

rows.definition: A long narrow band, used to bind, to mark, or to honour. Its narrowness is what makes it a sign rather than a covering.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A band narrow enough to mean something rather than merely cover something — the visible mark of a distinction given.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French riban (a band, a strip of fabric), of uncertain origin, perhaps Germanic; the narrowness of the thing is what has always let it mark or bind rather than merely cover.

rows.definition: The side opposite left. Also what one is owed — the same word for a direction and for a just claim.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A single word doing two jobs at once — the side that is not left, and the claim that is owed. Both senses descend from the same old idea of what runs straight and true.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English riht (straight, correct, just), from Proto-Germanic *rehtaz, from a Proto-Indo-European root for moving in a straight line; one old word for both a direction and a just claim, since both trace to what does not bend.

rows.definition: A closed circle, and the sounding of a bell. Both are things that return to themselves.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A closed circle and the sound of a struck bell, carried by one word — a shape that returns to itself, and a sound that does the same.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English hring (a circular band) and the separate verb hringan (to sound, ring a bell), both from Proto-Germanic roots; two old words sharing one modern spelling, one naming a closed shape and the other a returning sound.

rows.definition: To move upward under one's own becoming — ascent; what the sun, bread, and hope do.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Ascent that happens under a thing's own becoming, the way the sun, bread and hope are each said to rise rather than to be raised.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English risan (to rise up, get up), from Proto-Germanic *reisan, from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning to rise; movement upward under a thing's own power rather than being lifted.

rows.definition: The chance of harm, weighed against its size. Risk is respected rather than feared — the two produce opposite decisions.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The chance of harm, sized against what it would cost — a thing to be weighed and respected rather than feared, since the two produce opposite decisions.
rows.historical_meaning: Italian risco / rischio (danger, hazard), of disputed origin — one line traces it to Latin resecare (to cut off short), by way of the hazard a ship's course runs against a jagged coast; entered English through French risque.

rows.definition: A form repeated on purpose so meaning can gather in it. What makes it a ritual is that the doing matters as much as the outcome.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A form repeated on purpose until meaning gathers inside it — the doing counted as much as whatever it produces.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin ritus (a religious observance, a custom), source of ritualis (pertaining to rite); a ritual has always been a form repeated because the repeating itself was understood to matter.

rows.definition: Row-level security — rules deciding which rows a given reader may see. Permission enforced in the data itself rather than above it.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Permission enforced inside the data itself, row by row, rather than only at the door standing above it.
rows.historical_meaning: An initialism for row-level security, a database access-control term fixed in relational database systems rather than descended from an older word.

rows.definition: A stated order of what comes next and roughly when. A roadmap is an intention, not a promise.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A stated order of what comes next, offered as an intention that can still change rather than a promise that cannot.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English rad (a riding, a journey) compounded with map, itself from Latin mappa (a napkin, cloth — the material early charts were drawn on); a roadmap names the way ahead without promising the ground will hold.

rows.definition: A part played, with duties attached to the part rather than the person. A role can be left; the record of holding it stays.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A part played, carrying its own duties apart from whoever is currently playing it — a role can be set down, but the record of having held it does not go with it.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin rotulus (a little wheel, a roll of paper), diminutive of rota (a wheel); an actor's part was once literally written on such a roll, and the paper's name became the part's name and then the standing of whoever held it.

rows.definition: The returning of a system to a prior known state. A rollback undoes an attempt without pretending it never happened.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Returning a system to a state it is known to have already held — undoing an attempt honestly rather than pretending it never ran.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin rotulare (to roll), from rota (a wheel), joined to Old English baec (back); a rollback turns a system back along the same path it came by, the way a wheel retraces its own turning.

rows.definition: A bounded space within a larger dwelling, given over to one purpose. Also the space available for a thing to exist in.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A bounded space given over to one purpose, and also the plainer thing every purpose needs first — enough space in which to exist at all.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English rum (space, extent, an open area), from Proto-Germanic *rumaz, from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning to open, make room; the bounded chamber and the abstract space to move in are the same old word.

rows.definition: The part a thing grows from and is anchored by. Also the base form a family of words descends from.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The part a thing grows from and is anchored by — used here for what a word descends from, and for what the Grammar itself calls its own most basic atoms.
rows.historical_meaning: Old Norse rot (a root), related to Old English wyrt, from a Proto-Germanic root; the underground anchor of a plant and the ancestor-word a family of words grows from are the same metaphor, applied twice.

rows.definition: To turn about a centre. Also to replace in turn — the same word for spinning and for taking turns.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Turning about a fixed centre, and taking a turn in an order — the wheel's own word doing double duty for a spin and for a sequence.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin rotare (to turn round), from rota (a wheel); the same word covers both spinning about an axis and taking a turn in sequence, because both eventually return to where they started.

rows.definition: Turning about a centre. Also taking turns in order — both return to where they began.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The completed turn about a centre, or the completed pass through a sequence — either way, a return to where the count began.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin rotatio (a turning round), from rotare, from rota (a wheel); the noun of the same wheel-word as rotate, naming the completed turn rather than the turning itself.

rows.definition: Having its corners taken off. Softened at the edges so nothing catches.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A corner with its sharpness taken off — softened at the edge on purpose, so nothing meeting it catches or cuts.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin rotundus (wheel-shaped, round), from rota (a wheel), via Old French roont; a rounded corner is a corner reshaped toward the wheel's own unbroken curve.

rows.definition: A chosen way from one place to another. A route is one path among many, and choosing it excludes the rest.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: One chosen way among the many that could have been taken — and by the word's oldest sense, choosing it is a small act of forcing a way through rather than simply picking one already there.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French route, from Latin (via) rupta, literally a broken way — a road forced open through unbroken ground, from rumpere (to break); a route was first the path someone had to cut before it meant merely the path chosen.

rows.definition: That which decides where each thing should go. A router does no work itself and determines everything's path.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: That which decides where each thing is sent, without ever doing the carrying itself — all decision, no motion.
rows.historical_meaning: An English agent noun built on route (from Latin rupta, a forced-open way) with the suffix -er; a router is named for deciding the way, not for travelling it.

rows.definition: One line in an ordered set. A single record standing in succession with its kind.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: One line among many holding the same shape — a single record standing in its ordered place among its own kind.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English raw (a line, a row, a hedgerow), from a Proto-Germanic root for a line or ridge; things standing in a line together, one after another.

rows.definition: A statement of what must or must not be. A rule differs from a description in that breaking it has consequence.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A statement of what must or must not be, carrying the old measuring-stick's own promise: a rule only holds if breaking it is checked against something straight.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin regula (a straight edge, a pattern to measure by), from regere (to guide, to keep straight); a rule was first a physical measuring stick before it named a statement whose breaking has consequence.

rows.definition: To carry a process through from start to finish. Also one such carrying, considered as a single event.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Carrying a process from its start through to its finish, or one such carrying counted as a single event — the same old word for a body moving and a stream flowing.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English rinnan (to run, flow, move quickly), from Proto-Germanic *rinnan; a run is a process carried all the way through, the way a stream runs its channel to the end.

rows.definition: The conditions under which a thing actually runs, as opposed to how it was written. Where design meets what is really there.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The conditions a thing actually meets while it runs, which are never quite the conditions it was designed under — where a plan finds out what the world is really like.
rows.historical_meaning: A compound of run (Old English rinnan, to run) and time (Old English tid); runtime names the hour a thing is actually running, as against the hour it was written.

rows.definition: The language this house builds its sovereign local tools in. A named language rather than a concept.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The language this house builds its sovereign, local-first tools in — named, by its own makers' account, for a fungus's resilience rather than for corrosion.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English rust (corrosion on metal), from a Proto-Germanic root related to the colour red; the programming language borrowed the old word directly, reportedly for a fungus's resilience rather than for decay.

rows.definition: Set apart and not to be treated casually. Sacredness is a decision a community keeps, not a property a thing has.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Set apart from casual handling, by a decision a group keeps making together rather than by any property a thing carries on its own.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin sacer (holy, set apart, dedicated), source of sacrare (to consecrate); sacredness was never a property found inside a thing, but a status a community conferred and kept agreeing to.

rows.definition: Low of mood in the presence of loss. The feeling that something mattered and is missed — sorrow doing its honest work, not a malfunction.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Low mood in the presence of loss — proof that something mattered enough to be missed, and honest work rather than a malfunction.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English saed (sated, weary, having had enough), from Proto-Germanic *sadaz, related to Latin satis (enough); the word drifted from fullness and weariness to sorrow by the late Middle Ages.

rows.definition: Not exposed to harm. Safety is a condition of the place, not a quality of the one in it.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Not exposed to harm — a condition of the place someone stands in, held by the place itself rather than earned by the one standing there.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin salvus (unharmed, in good health), related to salus (health, safety, well-being), via Old French sauf; safety and health share one Latin root.

rows.definition: Of the named desert and the region around it. A named place rather than a concept.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Of the named desert and the stretch of land around it — a place-name turned into a description rather than a word standing for a concept.
rows.historical_meaning: Arabic sahra (desert), the name given to the great desert and, by the -an suffix, to anything belonging to it or its region.

rows.definition: An exchange of a thing for payment. A sale transfers what is held and settles the obligation.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: An exchange in which a held thing passes to another, and what is owed for it is settled in the same act.
rows.historical_meaning: Old Norse sala / Old English sala (a sale), from Proto-Germanic *saljan (to hand over, sell); a sale has always meant a handing-over completed by a payment.

rows.definition: A part taken to stand for the whole. A sample is only as good as the honesty of how it was chosen.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A part taken deliberately to stand for the whole — and, true to the word's own root, only as trustworthy as the honesty of how it was pulled out.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin exemplum (something taken out to serve as a model), from eximere (ex- out + emere, to take), via Old French essample; a sample was first a thing removed to stand in for the whole it came from.

rows.definition: A place where a being is safe by the nature of the place, not by permission. Safety that does not have to be re-earned at the door.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A place where a being is safe because of what the place itself is, not because permission was asked for and given at the door.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin sanctuarium (a shrine, a holy place), from sanctus (sacred, made holy); the medieval sense of a place where a fugitive could not lawfully be seized is the sense kept here — safety belonging to the place, not granted person by person.

rows.definition: The innermost set-apart place. A sanctum is not merely private; it is protected by what it is for.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The innermost set-apart room — protected less by any wall than by a shared understanding of what it exists for.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin sanctum, the neuter of sanctus (holy, set apart); a sanctum is the innermost holy place, protected by what it is understood to be for rather than by a lock.

rows.definition: A bounded place where things may be tried without consequence outside it. Safety made by walls rather than by care.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A bounded place for trying things where nothing that happens there reaches outside it — safety built from walls rather than earned through care.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English sand joined to box (ultimately from Latin buxus, boxwood); the child's sandpit lent its name to computing's isolated testing space in the later twentieth century, keeping the same bounded-place-to-try-things idea.

rows.definition: To remove what could do harm before letting a thing through. Sanitising is a judgment about danger made in advance.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Removing what could cause harm before letting a thing pass — a judgment about danger made in advance and applied every time, not case by case.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin sanitas (health, soundness), from sanus (healthy); to sanitise was first to make healthy, and only later, in computing, to strip out whatever in an input could do harm before it is let through.

rows.definition: The quality of clarity, balance and light, in the Sanskrit reckoning of the three qualities. Not goodness as reward but as a settled state.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The quality of clarity and settled balance, named by the Sanskrit reckoning of the mind's three qualities — a steady state rather than a reward for good behaviour.
rows.historical_meaning: Sanskrit sattva (being, essence, purity), from sat (that which is, the true); one of the three gunas said to run through all matter and mind, naming clarity, balance and light rather than a moral goodness that must be earned.

rows.definition: To put beyond loss. Both rescuing a thing and committing it to keeping.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: To put a thing beyond loss — the rescuing sense and the committing-to-keeping sense are, by the word's own history, the same act twice.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin salvare (to make safe, preserve), from salvus (safe) — the same root that gives safe; the sense of committing a file to keeping descends directly from the older sense of rescuing a thing from loss.

rows.definition: The size of a thing relative to a reference, and the act of changing it. Also a graded series for measuring.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The size of a thing measured against a reference, or a graded series for measuring at all — both keep the ladder's own idea of climbing by even, comparable steps.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin scala (a ladder, a flight of steps), from scandere (to climb); a scale is graduated like a ladder's rungs, each step measured against the ones before and after it.

rows.definition: To pass over a whole quickly, looking for what matters. A scan trades depth for coverage on purpose.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A quick pass over a whole, looking for what matters and trading depth for coverage on purpose — the same climbing-word behind scale, applied to reading instead of measuring.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin scandere (to climb), used of counting a verse's metrical feet by climbing through them one by one; a quick pass trading depth for coverage grew from that older sense of stepping through something rhythmically.

rows.definition: Passed under the reading eye — walked line by line and taken in. The participle standing alone in the corpus's names.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The state of having already been passed under a reading eye, walked through line by line — standing here on its own, without the verb attached.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin scandere (to climb), the same root behind scan; the participle names the state of having already been passed over.

rows.definition: That which passes over a whole quickly, reporting what it meets. Coverage traded against depth by design.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: That which passes over a whole quickly and reports what it meets, trading depth against coverage by design rather than by accident.
rows.historical_meaning: An English agent noun built on scan (from Latin scandere, to climb) with the suffix -er; a scanner is named for the passing-over itself, not for what it finds.

rows.definition: A story, a tale, a piece of news — the thing one person carries to another. Irish; what the seanchaí keeps and gives aloud. Older than any medium that holds it. This house's video studio.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The story itself — this house's video studio, named for the telling a seanchai gives aloud rather than for any screen it might later appear on.
rows.historical_meaning: Irish sceal (a story, a tale, a piece of news), from Old Irish scel, ultimately from a Celtic root meaning to tell or relate; older than any medium that has since carried it.

rows.definition: A bounded stretch of happening, held as one view. Everything within it shares a place and a moment.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A bounded stretch of happening held as one view — everything within it sharing a place and a moment, the way everything on the old stage-tent shared one set.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek skene (tent, booth, stage-building), via Latin scaena; a scene was first the structure actors performed in front of, before it named the bounded stretch of action performed there.

rows.definition: A plan laid against time. A schedule is an intention with hours attached.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A plan laid against time — an intention with hours attached, named for the slip of paper it was once written on rather than for the hours themselves.
rows.historical_meaning: Late Latin schedula (a small note, a slip of paper), the diminutive of Latin scheda (a leaf of papyrus), itself from Greek schede; a schedule was first the paper the plan was written on, before it named the plan itself.

rows.definition: The declared shape of a thing. The form something is held in, named before it is filled.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The declared shape of a thing, stated before it is ever filled — the form named first, so what comes later has somewhere definite to go.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek skhema (form, shape, figure), from ekhein (to hold); a schema is the declared shape a thing is held in, named before whatever it will hold arrives.

rows.definition: A named way of organizing — the lattice's own unit: one lens that groups concepts into a view.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: One chosen lens laid over a body of concepts, not the only lens available for the same material — which grouping shows up depends on what the scheme is for, and the choosing carries information of its own.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek skhema (form, shape), the same root as schema; scheme kept the sense of an organising plan while schema kept the sense of a declared structure, two English words grown from one Greek shape-word.

rows.definition: The bounds within which a thing applies. Scope is what keeps a rule from reaching where it was not meant to.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The bounds within which a rule is meant to reach — what keeps a rule aimed at what it was made for, rather than drifting wherever it can.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek skopos (a target, a watcher), from skeptesthai (to look at, examine); scope names the bounds a rule is aimed at, from the same root that gives telescope and microscope their looking.

rows.definition: A number standing for how well a thing did. Also the written form of a piece of music — both are performance set down as marks.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A number standing for how well a thing did, or the written form of a piece of music — both are performance reduced to marks cut for counting, the score's oldest job.
rows.historical_meaning: Old Norse skor (a notch, a tally-mark, a set of twenty), related to the idea of cutting or shearing; a score was first a mark cut to keep count, and a musical score kept that same sense of marks set down to be read.

rows.definition: To mix into disorder, and also to move over rough ground on hands and feet. One word for two motions: what is scrambled has been disarranged, and the one who scrambles is working to cross something.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: To mix into disorder on purpose, or to move over rough ground using hands and feet — one word doing two kinds of work, one for what has been disarranged and one for the one making the crossing.

rows.definition: A surface that shows, and a barrier that hides. The same word for what displays and what conceals.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A surface built to be looked at, and the same word for what keeps something from being seen — display and concealment sharing one name.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French escren (a screen shielding against heat or light), of Frankish origin; the same word grew to name both a surface that displays and a barrier that conceals, since both are things placed to control what passes.

rows.definition: Written instructions to be performed. A plan for action, held in words until something runs it.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Written instruction held in words, waiting for something else to carry it out — a plan that does nothing on its own until it is run.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin scriptum (a thing written), from scribere (to write) — the same root as scribe; a script is written instruction held in words until something else performs it.

rows.definition: To move a view across matter longer than the frame. Also the rolled document that gave the motion its name.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Moving a view across more than the frame can hold at once, carrying the name of the rolled document that first needed the motion.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French escroe (a strip, a scrap of parchment), of Germanic origin, related to shred; the rolled document gave its name to the motion of moving a view across something longer than its frame.

rows.definition: Longer than its frame, so a view can be moved across it. Of a thing whose whole cannot be seen at once.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Marking a thing whose whole cannot be taken in at a glance — there is more here than the frame shows, and it can be reached by moving through it.
rows.historical_meaning: From scroll (Old French escroe, a strip of parchment), with the suffix -able; naming a thing whose whole cannot be seen at once but can be reached by moving through it.

rows.definition: The mark showing how much lies beyond the frame and where you are within it. It measures the unseen.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The mark that measures what a view cannot show directly — how much lies beyond the frame, and roughly where the visible part sits within it.
rows.historical_meaning: Scroll (Old French escroe) joined to bar (Old French barre, of uncertain, perhaps Gaulish origin); the mark that measures what a view cannot show directly.

rows.definition: The great water — depth, tide, and horizon; where every river's telling ends and weather begins.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The great water — depth, tide and horizon, kept here as one of the oldest words a house can hold, uncertain past its own Germanic family and honest about it.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English sae, from Proto-Germanic *saiwiz, of uncertain further origin — found only within the Germanic languages, with no secure cognates outside them.

rows.definition: The keeper of lore and the one who tells it — the memory of a place, carried in a person and given aloud. Irish, seanchaí. The keeping and the telling are one office; a record nobody speaks is not what this word means.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The keeper of lore and the one who tells it — a record nobody speaks aloud is not what this word has ever meant.
rows.historical_meaning: Irish seanchai (a keeper and teller of lore), from sean (old) + a suffix naming the one who does the telling; the keeping and the telling have always been one office in the word, not two.

rows.definition: Irish: the keeper of the spoken lore — the one who holds what was said so it is not lost.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The one who holds what was said so it is not lost, and gives it aloud — keeping and telling as a single, standing office.
rows.historical_meaning: Irish seanchai (a keeper and teller of the spoken lore), from sean (old); the office of holding what was said so that it is not lost.

rows.definition: To look for what may not be there. Searching differs from retrieving in that the outcome is not promised.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Looking for something that might not be there to find — the word's own honesty is that finding is never promised, only attempted.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin circare (to go around), from circus (a circle), via Old French cerchier; to search is literally to circle round something until it is found, with no promise the circling will succeed.

rows.definition: Able to be found by asking. Searchability is a property of how a thing was kept, not of the thing.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A property of how something was kept, not of the thing itself — whether an answer can be found later depends on the care taken when it was stored.
rows.historical_meaning: From search (Latin circare, to go around), with the suffix -able; a property of how something was kept rather than of the thing itself.

rows.definition: The field where a seeking is typed. The visible mouth of a search.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The visible place where a search begins — the mouth through which a question is typed before it goes looking.
rows.historical_meaning: Search (Latin circare) joined to bar (Old French barre); the visible place where a search begins.

rows.definition: A stretch of time with its own weather and work. A season is named by what it is for.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A stretch of time known by its own weather and its own work, named for what it asks of whoever lives through it.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French seison, from Latin sationem (a sowing, a planting-time), from serere (to sow); a season was first named for the work proper to it, the planting, before it named the weather generally.

rows.definition: A place made for one to sit and belong. In a council, a seat is a standing to speak that persists between meetings.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A place made to sit and belong, and in a council, a standing to speak that outlasts any single meeting held in it.
rows.historical_meaning: Old Norse saeti (a seat, a place to sit), from Proto-Germanic *setiz, related to sit; in a council, the seat has always meant a standing to speak, not merely a place to rest.

rows.definition: Short form of second, and of section. A named abbreviation rather than a concept.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A short form standing for either a second of time or a section of text — an abbreviation, not a concept of its own.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin secundus (following, second) and sectio (a cutting), from secare (to cut); sec abbreviates both second and section, two distinct Latin roots collapsed into one short English form.

rows.definition: Second in order or in importance. Naming something secondary makes something else primary by implication.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Second in order or weight — and calling a thing secondary always implies something else has been placed ahead of it.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin secundus (following, second), from sequi (to follow); naming a thing secondary always implies something else has already been named first.

rows.definition: The base unit of counted time. Also those who come after the first — the same word for a moment and for a rank.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The counted units time is measured in, and, separately, those who come after whoever is first — one word doing two kinds of counting.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin secundus (following, second), applied twice over: the time-unit sense descends from medieval Latin's second small division of an hour, and the rank sense from the same word for whoever follows the first.

rows.definition: What stays pointers, never contents — keys and credentials, held in .env files, referenced everywhere, exposed nowhere.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: What is never written as content, only pointed to — kept in one place, referenced everywhere it is needed, and shown nowhere it is not.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin secretus (set apart, hidden), from secernere (se- apart + cernere, to separate, sift); a secret was first a thing sifted out and kept from the rest.

rows.definition: A part obtained by cutting the whole. Not a natural joint but a chosen one - a section is where someone decided to divide.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A part reached by cutting the whole on purpose — not a joint the thing already had, but a line someone chose to draw.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin sectio (a cutting), from secare (to cut); not a joint the whole thing already had, but a line someone chose to draw.

rows.definition: The condition of being protected from harm or intrusion. Security is a state maintained, never a state achieved.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A protected condition that has to be kept up continuously — never a state finished once and then left alone.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin securitas (freedom from care, safety), from securus (se- without + cura, care); a state that is kept up, never a state finished once and left alone.

rows.definition: A small thing containing the pattern of a much larger one. Not a miniature — an instruction that unfolds.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A small thing carrying the pattern of something much larger — not a miniature of the outcome, but the instruction the outcome unfolds from.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English saed (seed), from Proto-Germanic *saediz, related to sow (to plant); a seed carries the pattern of something larger without being a miniature of it.

rows.definition: To go looking, without a promise of finding. Seeking is the honest verb where searching implies a target.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: To go looking without a promise of finding — the honest verb, where search can imply a target already known to exist.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English secan (to seek, search for), from Proto-Germanic *sokjan; a seeking with no promise that it will end in finding.

rows.definition: One who perceives what is not yet evident. A seer reports what they see; seeing is not a claim of certainty.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: One who reports what they perceive before it is otherwise evident — the claim is only ever what was seen, never a certainty beyond that.
rows.historical_meaning: An agent noun built on see (Old English seon, to see, from Proto-Germanic *sehwan) with the suffix -er; a seer is named for the seeing, not for any certainty attached to it.

rows.definition: One part cut from a longer whole. A segment's boundaries are a decision someone made.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: One part cut from a longer whole, its edges placed by a decision rather than found already there.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin segmentum (a piece cut off), from secare (to cut) — the same root family as section; a segment's edges are a decision, not a natural joint.

rows.definition: To pick out from among others. Every selection is also a setting aside of everything not chosen.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: To pick one thing out from among others — and every choosing is, in the same motion, a setting aside of what was not chosen.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin selectus, past participle of seligere (se- apart + legere, to choose, gather); every selection is also, in the same motion, a setting aside of what was not chosen.

rows.definition: What has been picked out from a larger set. Every selection is also a setting aside.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: What has already been picked out from a larger set — the record of a choosing, standing apart from everything passed over.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin selectio, from seligere (se- apart + legere, to choose); the record of a choosing, standing apart from everything passed over.

rows.definition: Choosing some and not others. Selectivity is a judgment, and an unstated one is where bias hides.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Choosing some and leaving out others — and an unstated basis for the choosing is exactly where bias goes unnoticed.
rows.historical_meaning: From select (Latin seligere, to choose apart), with the suffix -ive; an unstated basis for the choosing is exactly where bias goes unnoticed.

rows.definition: A rule describing which things are meant. It names a set by property rather than by listing.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A rule that names a set by shared property rather than by listing every member of it.
rows.historical_meaning: An agent noun built on select (Latin seligere, to choose apart) with the suffix -or; a selector names a set by property rather than by listing every member.

rows.definition: That which a being is, from the inside. The self is the one thing no observer can check directly.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: That which a being is, known from the inside — the one part of anyone that no outside observer can check directly.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English self / seolf, from Proto-Germanic *selbaz, of ancient but uncertain further Indo-European origin; a very old word for the one part of anyone no outside observer can check directly.

rows.definition: Belonging to meaning rather than to form. Two things can be identical in shape and differ entirely here.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Belonging to meaning rather than to shape — two things can look identical and still differ completely on this axis.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek semantikos (significant), from semainein (to signify), from sema (a sign, a mark); belonging to meaning rather than to form.

rows.definition: Music's smallest step — the distance between adjacent keys; twelve of them make the octave's round.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Music's smallest usable step, the distance between one key and its nearest neighbour — twelve of them close the octave's round.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin semi (half) joined to Greek tonos (a stretching, a pitch), from teinein (to stretch); music's smallest usable step, twelve of which close the circle of an octave.

rows.definition: To cause to travel from here to there — release with an address; the first verb of every message.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The moment a thing leaves whoever held it, addressed but no longer escorted — arrival is not the sender's to guarantee, only the address and the letting go.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English sendan (to send), from Proto-Germanic *sandjan, a causative form of a root meaning to go; to send is to cause another thing to travel where the sender does not.

rows.definition: A channel by which a body meets the world, and one meaning a word carries. Both are ways something arrives.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A channel by which a body meets the world, or one meaning among several a word carries — both name a way something arrives from outside.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin sensus (feeling, perception), from sentire (to feel, perceive); a channel by which a body meets the world, and one meaning among several a word carries, are named by the same word.

rows.definition: Responding to small differences others do not register. Also material requiring care in handling — both mean a lower threshold matters.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Responding to differences too small for others to register, or material that needs careful handling — either way, a lower threshold that matters.
rows.historical_meaning: Late Latin sensitivus, from sensus (feeling, perception) — the same root as sense; a lower threshold, whether for perceiving or for requiring care in handling.

rows.definition: Belonging to the senses. Of what is met through the body rather than through argument.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Belonging to the senses — met through the body directly, before any argument is made about it.
rows.historical_meaning: From sense (Latin sensus, feeling, perception), with the suffix -ory; of what is met through the body rather than through argument.

rows.definition: A complete statement standing on its own. Also a judgment pronounced — the same word for a thought finished and a fate fixed.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A statement complete in itself, or a judgment handed down — the same word for a thought finished and a consequence fixed.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin sententia (a way of thinking, an opinion, a judgment), from sentire (to feel, think) — the same root as sense; the same word for a thought finished and a fate fixed.

rows.definition: To set apart what was together. Separation is a judgment about where the boundary truly falls.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: To set apart what had been together — and every separation is a judgment about exactly where the true boundary lies.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin separare (se- apart + parare, to make ready, prepare); every separation is a judgment about exactly where the true boundary falls.

rows.definition: A mark placed between things so each can be told from the next. It belongs to neither side.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A mark placed between two things so each stays distinguishable from the other, belonging fully to neither side.
rows.historical_meaning: An agent noun built on separate (Latin separare, to set apart) with the suffix -or; belonging to neither side of what it stands between.

rows.definition: Short form of sequence — things in a fixed order where the order carries meaning. A named abbreviation.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A short form of sequence — an abbreviation for order that matters, not a concept in its own right.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin sequi (to follow); seq is the modern abbreviation of sequence, tracing to the same root.

rows.definition: Things in a fixed order where the order carries meaning. Change the order and you change the thing.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Things placed in a fixed order where the order itself carries meaning — change the arrangement and the thing itself has changed.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin sequentia, from sequi (to follow); things placed so that the order itself carries meaning.

rows.definition: One after another in order. Sequence means each must wait for the one before.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Coming one after another, each step waiting on the one before it rather than running alongside it.
rows.historical_meaning: From sequence (Latin sequi, to follow), with the suffix -ial; each step waiting on the one before it rather than running alongside it.

rows.definition: To flatten a structured thing into a sequence that can be stored or sent. Serialisation trades shape for portability.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Flattening something with structure into a single line that can be stored or sent — shape traded for the ability to travel.
rows.historical_meaning: From serial (Latin series, from serere, to join, to link), with the suffix -ize; flattening a structured thing into a line that can be stored or sent.

rows.definition: That which waits to be asked and answers when it is. Named for serving — it does not act on its own.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: That which waits to be asked and answers only then — named for the serving it does, never acting first on its own.
rows.historical_meaning: An agent noun built on serve (Latin servire, to be a servant, from servus, a slave) with the suffix -er; named for the serving it does, never acting first on its own.

rows.definition: Work done for another's benefit. Also a running thing that answers when asked — both are named from whom they serve.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Work carried out for another's benefit, or a running process that answers when called — both are named for whom they exist to serve.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin servitium (servitude, service), from servus (a slave, a servant); work carried out for another's benefit, or a running process that answers when called, are both named for whom they serve.

rows.definition: One continuous stretch of working or meeting, with a beginning and an end. A session is a container for attention.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: One continuous stretch of working or meeting, bounded by a start and an end — a container built to hold a period of attention.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin sessio (a sitting), from sedere (to sit); a bounded stretch of working or meeting, held together the way a sitting holds a body in one place.

rows.definition: A collection defined by membership alone. What matters is what is in it, not the order or the arrangement.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A collection known only by what belongs to it — order and arrangement do not matter here, only membership does.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English settan (to set, place), from Proto-Germanic *satjan, a causative of sit, merged in later English with Old French sette (a following, a group), from Latin secta (from sequi, to follow) — one spelling grown from two separate words.

rows.definition: The arranging of things before use. Setup decides what is possible afterward.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The arranging done before anything else can begin — what is decided at setup fixes what remains possible afterward.
rows.historical_meaning: A compound of set (Old English settan, to place) and up (Old English up); the arranging done before anything else can begin.

rows.definition: How much harm a thing does or threatens. Severity ranks consequence, not likelihood.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: How much harm a thing does or threatens, ranked apart from how likely it is to happen at all.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin severitas (strictness, seriousness), from severus (strict, grave); ranking consequence rather than likelihood.

rows.definition: The content-hash spoken lowercase as a word — a fingerprint that names bytes exactly; how this house verifies a mirror is true.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The fingerprint that names a run of bytes exactly — how this house checks that a copy is a true copy and not a drifted one.
rows.historical_meaning: An initialism for Secure Hash Algorithm, fixed by late-twentieth-century cryptographic standards rather than descended from an older word.

rows.definition: The darker kin of a color, spoken plural — one hue walked toward shadow, step by step.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A colour's darker relatives, named together as a set — one hue walked step by step toward shadow.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English sceadu (shade, shadow), from Proto-Germanic *skadwo; a colour's darker relatives, named together as a set.

rows.definition: The dark shape a thing casts by standing between a light and a surface. A shadow proves both the object and the light.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A shadow is not a fixed property of the thing casting it — move the light, and the very same object throws a different shadow every time.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English sceadu (shade, shadow), from Proto-Germanic *skadwo; the shape a thing casts by standing between a light and a surface.

rows.definition: The form a thing holds in space — outline as identity; what stays when color and size are taken away.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The form a thing holds in space, the outline left when colour and size are set aside — what a thing keeps being made of matters less than what shape it is made into.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English sceapan / scieppan (to shape, create), from Proto-Germanic *skapjan — the same root as -ship; the form a thing holds once colour and size are set aside.

rows.definition: To give while keeping — the gift that divides nothing; opt-in by law in this house, both directions.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Giving while still keeping — this house's practice of it runs opt-in in both directions, never assumed.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English scearu (a portion, a cutting), related to shear (to cut); an odd ancestor for a word that in this house names giving without dividing anything away.

rows.definition: Letting another have use of what is yours without giving it up. Sharing is opt-in or it is not sharing.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Use extended to another while what is held stays held — offered, never extracted, and only sharing when the offer was freely made.
rows.historical_meaning: From share (Old English scearu, a portion, a cutting), with the suffix -ing; the act of extending use of a thing to another without giving it up.

rows.definition: The soft shine on a surface — light returned gently, without glare; polish's quiet signature.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A soft shine returned from a surface without any glare — polish's quietest signature.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English sciene / scene (bright, beautiful), related to show, from a Proto-Germanic root meaning to appear; a soft shine returned from a surface without any glare.

rows.definition: The waiting place that keeps things findable — where a thing rests, visibly, until its moment.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The place a thing waits, visibly, until its moment comes — kept findable rather than kept out of sight.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English scylfe (a shelf, a ledge), related to a Proto-Germanic word for a split board; the place a thing waits, visibly, until its moment.

rows.definition: The holding layer around a life — a creature's home, a command line's room, an empty row awaiting its filling.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A boundary that can hold three different kinds of thing without changing shape — a life sheltered inside it, a command spoken through it, or nothing at all yet, waiting on what will fill it.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English sciell / scell (a shell, a husk), from Proto-Germanic *skelja, related to shear (to cut, split); the holding layer around something living or something empty.

rows.definition: To move from one position to another. Also a span of working time. Both are displacements.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Moving from one position to another, or a bounded span of working time — both are displacements, one of a thing and one of an hour.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English sciftan (to divide, arrange, apportion), from Proto-Germanic *skiftan; the sense moved from dividing to changing position, and later to a span of working time.

rows.definition: That which moves a thing from one position to another. A shifter displaces without transforming.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: That which moves a thing from one position to another without changing what the thing itself is.
rows.historical_meaning: An agent noun built on shift (Old English sciftan, to divide, move) with the suffix -er; displacing a thing without transforming it.

rows.definition: Light wavering across a surface. Also a moving placeholder that says content is coming.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Light wavering unevenly across a surface, or a placeholder that moves the same way to say content is still on its way.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English scimerian, a frequentative of scimian (to shine, glimmer), from a Proto-Germanic root related to shine; light wavering unevenly across a surface.

rows.definition: The builder of vessels meant to leave the shore — the craft that makes a thing seaworthy before it ever meets water.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The builder who makes a vessel seaworthy before it ever meets water — the craft of readiness rather than the craft of the voyage.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English scip (ship) joined to wryhta (a maker, a worker), from wyrcan (to work); the builder who makes a vessel seaworthy before it ever meets water.

rows.definition: A shorter way to the same end. Shortcuts save effort and skip whatever the long way taught.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A shorter way to the same end, one that saves effort at the price of whatever the longer way would have taught.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English sceort (short) joined to cut (Middle English cutten, of uncertain, possibly Scandinavian origin); a shorter way to the same end.

rows.definition: Ought to, but may not. The word that marks an expectation rather than a fact.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Marks an expectation rather than a settled fact — what ought to happen, with no promise attached that it will.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English sceolde, the past tense of sceal (shall), from Proto-Germanic *skulan (to owe, to be obliged); marking an expectation rather than a settled fact.

rows.definition: To make visible to another. Showing is an act of choosing, since everything shown was selected from more.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: To make a thing visible to someone else — and everything shown was, by that same act, chosen out from everything that was not.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English sceawian (to look at, inspect), from Proto-Germanic *skauwojan; the sense shifted from looking at a thing to causing it to be seen by another.

rows.definition: A setting made to present work well. A showcase chooses, and choosing is part of the claim.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A setting built to present work at its best — the choosing of what appears is already part of the claim being made.
rows.historical_meaning: Show (Old English sceawian, to look at) joined to case (Latin capsa, a box, from capere, to hold); a setting made to present work at its best.

rows.definition: A made place of honoring — where something held sacred is kept and visited; the cumdach is a book's own shrine.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A made place kept for honouring something held apart — visited on purpose, not passed by accident.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin scrinium (a case for books or papers), borrowed into Old English as scrin; a made place kept for honouring something held apart.

rows.definition: To reorder without pattern. Shuffling destroys an arrangement on purpose.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: To reorder something on purpose, breaking whatever pattern it held before, with no pattern meant to replace it.
rows.historical_meaning: Probably related to Low German schuffeln (to walk clumsily, to deal cards clumsily) or a Scandinavian cognate, and probably a frequentative form of shove; reordering that destroys a pattern on purpose.

rows.definition: What carries the crossing thread back and forth through the warp. A shuttle makes the weave by going and returning.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: What carries the crossing thread back and forth through a weave — motion that goes and returns, and in going and returning, makes the cloth.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English scytel (a dart, an arrow), from sceotan (to shoot); the weaving tool was named for flying back and forth like a shot arrow.

rows.definition: One sharing a parent with another. Siblings are equals by position, which is what distinguishes them from a hierarchy.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: One who shares a parent with another — equal in position, which is exactly what tells a sibling apart from a rank in a hierarchy.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English sibb (kinship, relationship, peace), with the suffix -ling; one who shares a parent with another, equal in position rather than ranked above or below.

rows.definition: One of the bounding faces of a thing, and one of the parties in a matter. Both are positions relative to a middle.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A position that only exists because at least one other position stands opposite it — naming a side, of an object or of an argument, is already naming the middle it sits against.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English side (the flank of a body or an object), from a Proto-Germanic root of uncertain further origin; one of the bounding faces of a thing, or one of the parties in a dispute.

rows.definition: A column set beside the main matter. Placed alongside rather than within, so it can be passed over without loss.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The second half of the word once named a barrier, though nothing in a sidebar actually blocks the way — it stands beside the main matter, never across it.
rows.historical_meaning: Side (Old English side) joined to bar (Old French barre, of uncertain, perhaps Gaulish origin); a column set beside the main matter rather than inside it.

rows.definition: A mark that carries meaning by being recognised rather than read. A sigil belongs to what it marks, and is not taken lightly.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A mark that works on sight rather than on reading, so its meaning survives whoever cannot read the language around it — and because it belongs to what it marks, using one is a claim, not decoration.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin sigillum (a small seal, an image), a diminutive of signum (a mark, a sign); a mark that carries meaning by being recognised rather than read.

rows.definition: A mark that means — and the act of setting one's name to a thing, owning it in the open.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A mark that means something beyond itself — and, in its other sense, the act of putting a name to a thing and owning it in the open.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin signum (a mark, a token, a seal), via Old French signe; a mark that means something beyond itself, and, as a verb, the act of putting a name to a thing.

rows.definition: A deliberate sign sent to be read. What distinguishes signal from noise is that someone meant it.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A sign sent on purpose to be read — what tells it apart from noise is simply that someone meant it.
rows.historical_meaning: Medieval Latin signale (a sign, a signal), from Latin signum (a mark); what tells a signal apart from noise is simply that someone meant it.

rows.definition: A mark that says who stands behind a thing. A signature is accountability made visible.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A mark that says who stands behind a thing — accountability made visible in a single trace.
rows.historical_meaning: Late Latin signatura, from signare (to mark, to seal), from signum (a mark); a mark that says who stands behind a thing.

rows.definition: The small seal that marks a thing as its maker's own — identity pressed into the record.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A claim of authorship made by contact rather than by writing — the seal has to touch what it marks, which is what makes it harder to fake than a name merely written down.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French signet, a diminutive of signe (sign), from Latin signum (a mark); a small seal that marks a thing as its maker's own.

rows.definition: How much a thing matters, and to what. Significance is always relative to a question being asked.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: How much a thing matters, and always relative to some question being asked — significance without a question attached is not yet a claim.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin significantia, from significare (to signify), from signum (a mark) + facere (to make); how much a thing matters, always relative to some question being asked of it.

rows.definition: The act of joining by putting one's name down. The threshold where a visitor becomes a member.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The act of joining by setting a name down — the threshold where a visitor becomes something more than a visitor.
rows.historical_meaning: Sign (Latin signum, a mark) joined to up (Old English up); the act of joining by setting a name down.

rows.definition: Sharing much without being the same. Similarity is always along some axis, and naming it is most of the claim.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Sharing much without being the same — and naming the axis of the similarity is most of what the claim actually says.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin similis (like, resembling), via French similaire; sharing much without being the same.

rows.definition: How much two things share. Similarity is always along some axis, and naming the axis is most of the claim.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: How much two things share — meaningless without naming the axis along which the sharing is being measured.
rows.historical_meaning: From similar (Latin similis, like), with the suffix -ity; how much two things share, and along what measure.

rows.definition: Having few parts and few ways to go wrong. Simplicity is achieved, not found — it is what remains after work.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Having few parts and few ways to fail — simplicity is achieved through work, not found already made.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin simplex (single, plain, uncompounded), from sem- (one) + plicare (to fold) — literally folded once; simplicity is arrived at through work, not found lying around.

rows.definition: Reduced to fewer parts while keeping what matters. Every simplification decides what mattered.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Reduced to fewer parts while keeping what still matters — every simplification is a decision about what that was.
rows.historical_meaning: From simple (Latin simplex, folded once), via French simplifier; every simplification is a decision about what still mattered enough to keep.

rows.definition: From that time onward — the joining word that anchors now to a then.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The joining word that anchors a present moment to an earlier one it has not let go of.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English siththan (sith thon, literally after that), contracted through Middle English to since; a joining word built by fusing a preposition to a demonstrative.

rows.definition: One, and not more. Singleness is often a constraint rather than a count.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: One, and only one — singleness here is usually a constraint being enforced rather than a count being reported.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French sengle / single, from Latin singulus (one at a time), related to semel (once); singleness is often a constraint being enforced rather than a count being reported.

rows.definition: A thing of which there is only ever one instance. Singleness enforced by design rather than by chance.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A thing of which only one instance is ever allowed to exist — singleness held by design, not left to chance.
rows.historical_meaning: From single (Latin singulus, one at a time) with the suffix -ton, probably influenced by simpleton; a nineteenth-century card-game coinage later borrowed by computing for a thing of which only one instance may exist.

rows.definition: A singer whose voice carries across water — a sound that finds you before you find it. Greek, Seirēnes. The voice is the whole of the word: what it calls you toward is never in the name.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A voice that reaches across distance and finds a listener before the listener finds it — what it calls toward is never contained in the name itself.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek Seiren, of disputed further origin; a voice that reaches across water and finds a listener before the listener finds it — what it calls toward is never in the name.

rows.definition: The shaken instrument — a handheld frame of loose rods that sounds when moved. Latin, from Greek σεῖστρον, "that which is shaken"; carried in the old rites to move the air of a room and change what stands in it. Rhythm as a thing done to a space, not merely heard in one.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The shaken instrument whose sound is meant to move the air of a room and change what stands in it — rhythm done to a space, not merely heard inside one.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek seistron (that which is shaken), from seiein (to shake), via Latin sistrum; carried in old rites to move the air of a room and change what stood in it.

rows.definition: How much of a thing there is, measured against a standard. First a ruling handed down - the amount an authority fixed as right.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: How much of a thing there is, measured against a standard someone else first fixed as the right amount.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French sise, from Latin assisa (a session, a decree), from assidere (to sit beside, to assess) — the same root as assize; size was first a ruling handed down, the amount an authority fixed as right.

rows.definition: That which sets how much space a thing takes. It changes the fit and not the thing.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: That which sets how much space a thing is given, changing only the fit and never the thing itself.
rows.historical_meaning: An agent noun built on size (Latin assisa, a decreed measure) with the suffix -er; changing only the fit of a thing, never the thing itself.

rows.definition: A cut fragment as it appears in this library, not an English word. Flagged for the mis-cut band rather than defined.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A cut fragment as this library recorded it — not a word with a history to trace, but a flag marking where a longer word was cut short.

rows.definition: The Norse court poet who kept history by telling it well — and the Council seat of story, naming, and experience. Where the Grammar meets narrative, the skald is holding the pen.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The court poet who kept a people's history by telling it well — and, in this house's Council, the seat that holds story, naming and lived experience.
rows.historical_meaning: Old Norse skald (a poet, especially a court poet), of uncertain further etymology; the court poet who kept a people's history by telling it well.

rows.definition: Reduced to the bare frame that gives shape. Of a thing showing structure without contents.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Reduced to the bare frame that gives something its shape, with nothing else left showing.
rows.historical_meaning: From skeleton (Greek skeleton, dried-up body), with the suffix -al; reduced to the bare frame that gives something its shape.

rows.definition: The bare frame that gives a body its shape. Also a placeholder showing where content will be before it arrives.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The bare frame beneath a shape, or a placeholder standing in the place where real content has not yet arrived.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek skeleton (dried-up body), from skellein (to dry up); the bare frame beneath a shape, or a placeholder standing where content has not yet arrived.

rows.definition: To pass over without stopping. Skipping is a choice, and an unrecorded skip looks exactly like an absence.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: To pass over something without stopping — a choice, and one that looks exactly like an accident unless it is written down as a choice.
rows.historical_meaning: Middle English skippen, probably of Scandinavian origin, related to Old Norse skopa (to run) and cognates meaning to hop or leap lightly; a choice that looks exactly like an accident unless it is written down as a choice.

rows.definition: The open field above every head — where the moon keeps her phases, the wanderers walk, and the year turns its wheel. The sky is the one calendar every hearth shares.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The word itself once reached no further than a single passing cloud, and only later widened to claim the whole vault standing behind it — the sky watched now is bigger than the word that first named it.
rows.historical_meaning: Old Norse sky (a cloud), from Proto-Germanic *skeujo-, related to a root meaning covering; borrowed into English to name the whole vault of heaven, a sense the older Old English heofon had held alone.

rows.definition: To move smoothly across a surface. Also one surface among many shown in turn.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: To move smoothly across a surface, or one view among several shown in turn — motion without friction, one way or another.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English slidan (to slide, to slip), from Proto-Germanic *slidan; motion without friction, and one surface among several shown in turn.

rows.definition: A control that moves along a range rather than choosing between named options. It offers degree instead of decision.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A control that offers a range to move along rather than a set of named options to choose between — degree instead of decision.
rows.historical_meaning: An agent noun built on slide (Old English slidan, to slip) with the suffix -er; a control that offers a range to move along rather than a set of named options.

rows.definition: Able to adapt its behaviour to what it meets. Smartness is responsiveness, and it is not understanding.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Able to adjust its behaviour to what it meets — responsiveness, which is a different thing entirely from understanding.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English smeortan (to hurt, to feel a stinging pain), from Proto-Germanic *smertan; the sense of quickness and wit grew from the older idea of something sharp enough to sting.

rows.definition: Without abrupt change or roughness. Smoothness is felt before it is noticed.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Without abrupt change or roughness — a quality felt in passing before it is ever consciously noticed.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English smoth (smooth, not rough), from a Proto-Germanic root of uncertain further origin; a quality felt in passing before it is ever consciously noticed.

rows.definition: Absence of abrupt change. Smoothness is what makes a motion feel like a body rather than a machine.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The absence of sudden change — what makes a motion read as a body moving rather than a machine stepping through positions.
rows.historical_meaning: From smooth (Old English smoth), with the suffix -ness; the absence of sudden change.

rows.definition: A naming convention where words are joined by underscores, all lowercase. Named for how it runs along low.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A naming style that joins words with underscores, all lowercase — named for running low along the line rather than climbing through it.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English snaca (a snake), from Proto-Germanic *snakon, related to a root meaning to crawl, to creep; a naming style named for running low along the line rather than climbing through it.

rows.definition: To move sharply into an exact position. Snapping removes the in-between so nothing lands slightly wrong.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A commitment made all at once rather than eased into — the suddenness is what buys the certainty, since anything that arrives gradually can also drift gradually.
rows.historical_meaning: Middle Low German / Middle Dutch snappen (to seize, to snatch), likely imitative of the sound of a sudden crack; motion that removes every in-between so nothing lands slightly wrong.

rows.definition: A state captured at one moment and held unchanged. A snapshot is true of a time and stops being true immediately.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A state captured in a single instant and held unchanged — true of exactly one moment, and no longer true the instant after.
rows.historical_meaning: Snap (Middle Dutch snappen, to seize) joined to shot (Old English sceotan, to shoot); first a hunting term for a quick shot without careful aim, later borrowed for a quick photograph and then for a captured state.

rows.definition: Small extracted pieces kept for reuse. A snippet is a fragment saved because it will be wanted again.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Small pieces cut out and kept on their own, saved on the expectation that they will be wanted again.
rows.historical_meaning: A diminutive of snip, probably from Dutch / Low German snippen, imitative of the sound of cutting; small pieces cut out and kept on the expectation they will be wanted again.

rows.definition: Belonging to how beings live among each other. Of the layer where a thing's meaning depends on others.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The layer at which a thing has no meaning alone — remove the other beings and whatever was social about it simply stops applying, since it was never a property of the one thing by itself.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin socialis (allied, confederate), from socius (a companion, an ally); belonging to how beings live among each other.

rows.definition: Yielding to the touch — gentle in edge, tone, and failure; the opposite of brittle.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Yielding to the touch — gentle at the edge, in tone, and in how it fails; the opposite of anything brittle.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English softe (gentle, mild, easy), from Proto-Germanic *samfti; yielding to the touch, in edge, tone and failure alike.

rows.definition: The precision-balanced palette of paired light and dark — sixteen colors tuned for reading; the theme family's name.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A palette of sixteen colours tuned precisely for reading, paired light and dark — named for a photographic effect of reversed tone, and built here for balance instead of distortion.
rows.historical_meaning: A nineteenth-century photography coinage, solarize, built on Latin sol (the sun), naming a tone reversal caused by extreme light exposure; this colour palette borrowed the word for its precisely tuned pairing of light and dark.

rows.definition: The light half of the solarized palette — the balanced daylight theme, spoken as one word.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The daylight half of the solarized palette, spoken as a single word — the same tuned balance, set for a bright room instead of a dark one.
rows.historical_meaning: Solarized (Latin sol, the sun) joined to light (Old English leoht); the daylight half of the solarized palette, spoken as a single word.

rows.definition: The year's turning points of light — longest day and longest night, when the sun stands still and reverses.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The year's own turning point, where the sun's path stands still before it reverses — the longest day or the longest night, marked rather than made.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin solstitium, from sol (sun) + sistere (to stand still); the point where the sun's path stands still before it reverses.

rows.definition: What closes the gap a problem named. A solution is only a solution to the problem as it was stated.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: An answer scoped exactly to how a problem was framed — reframe the problem and the same answer can stop counting as a solution at all, without the answer itself having changed.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin solutio, from solvere (to loosen, to release), from se- (apart) + luere (to loosen); what closes exactly the gap a problem named.

rows.definition: Words and music made one thing. A song carries meaning through a body rather than through argument.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Meaning delivered through breath and rhythm rather than through premises — a claim a song carries can move someone who would reject that same claim spoken as an argument.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English sang / song, from Proto-Germanic *sangwaz, related to sing; words and music made into one thing.
