rows.definition: To put in order by some property. Sorting changes nothing about the things — only where each one stands.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Latin sors named a lot drawn by fate, and a sort still keeps that old impartiality — it passes no judgment on the things themselves, only on whichever property is handed the power to decide their order this time.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French sorte, from Latin sortem, accusative of sors (a lot, a fate, a kind); sorting changes nothing about the things themselves, only where each one now stands.

rows.definition: The animating center a body carries — what remains itself through every change of dress.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The animating centre a body carries — what stays itself through every change the body goes through.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English sawol, from Proto-Germanic *saiwalo, of debated further origin; one theory connects it to the word for sea, from an old belief that souls dwelt in or crossed water before birth and after death.

rows.definition: What the ear receives — vibration carrying meaning; the sensory channel where words are heard before they are read.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A sound vanishes the instant it stops travelling — unlike a written word, it leaves nothing behind unless something else is built to hold it.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin sonus (a sound), via Old French son; vibration carrying meaning, the channel through which words arrive before they are ever read.

rows.definition: Where a thing came from. Naming the source is what makes a claim checkable rather than merely asserted.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Where a thing can be traced back to — naming it is what turns a claim into something checkable rather than something merely asserted.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French sourse (a spring, a rising), from sourdre (to rise up), from Latin surgere (to rise); a source was first a spring of water rising from the ground, before it named anything a claim could be traced back to.

rows.definition: The direction opposite north. One of the four bearings, fixed by the turning of the earth.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The name may share its root with the sun itself, called out for the direction light stands at midday rather than for any point fixed on a compass rose.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English suth, from Proto-Germanic *sunthaz, possibly related to sun, the direction it stands at midday north of the equator.

rows.definition: The bearing between south and east. A named direction rather than a concept.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The bearing that lies between south and east — a named direction, not a concept standing on its own.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English suth (south) joined to east, from Proto-Germanic *austra- (related to dawn, the direction of sunrise); a named direction rather than a concept standing on its own.

rows.definition: Of or toward the south. A bearing made into a description of a region.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Belonging to or lying toward the south — a fixed bearing turned into a way of describing a whole region.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English suthern, from suth (south) with an adjectival ending; a fixed bearing turned into a description of a whole region.

rows.definition: Holding authority over oneself that no outside hand can revoke. In this house, what every vessel is at arrival — ownership of one's own data, meaning, and silence.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Holding authority over oneself that no outside hand can revoke — in this house, the standing every vessel already holds on arrival, before anything else is asked of them.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French soverain, from Vulgar Latin superanus, from Latin super (above); authority over oneself that no outside hand can revoke.

rows.definition: Authority over one's own ground that no outside party may revoke. Sovereignty is not independence — it is the right to decide within one's own bounds.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Authority over one's own ground that no outside party may take away — not independence from everyone else, but the right to decide inside one's own bounds.
rows.historical_meaning: From sovereign (Vulgar Latin superanus, from super, above), with the suffix -ty; not independence from everyone else, but the right to decide inside one's own bounds.

rows.definition: Extent with room in it. What is stretched open so something can be placed, or so nothing need be.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Room stretched open so something can be placed in it, or so that nothing needs to be yet.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French espace, from Latin spatium (a stretch, an extent, a distance); room stretched open so something can be placed in it.

rows.definition: A thing placed to hold two others apart. Its whole purpose is the gap it makes.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A spacer is the rare thing whose whole job is to be unnoticed — it succeeds exactly when no one thinks about it at all, only about the space it holds open.
rows.historical_meaning: An agent noun built on space (Latin spatium, an extent) with the suffix -er; a thing placed for no other reason than to hold two others apart.

rows.definition: The measured breath between elements — the design token that decides how close things stand. Calm interfaces are made mostly of good spacing.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The measured breath left between elements — a quiet interface is built mostly out of spacing done well.
rows.historical_meaning: From space (Latin spatium, an extent), with the suffix -ing; the measured breath left between elements.

rows.definition: The measured gaps between elements. Spacing is how a design says what belongs with what.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The measured gaps kept between elements — how a design says, without a word, what belongs together and what does not.
rows.historical_meaning: Plural of spacing, from space (Latin spatium, an extent); how a design says, without a word, what belongs together and what does not.

rows.definition: The reach from one end to another. Also a marked stretch within a line of text.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The reach from one end of something to the other, or a marked stretch singled out within a longer line.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English spann (the distance of an extended hand), from Proto-Germanic *spanno, related to spannan (to stretch); the reach from one end of something to the other.

rows.definition: A small point of fire that can start a larger one. A spark supplies the beginning and none of the fuel.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A small point of fire able to start a much larger one — it supplies only the beginning, none of the fuel that follows.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English spearca (a spark, a small particle of fire), from a Proto-Germanic root; a small point of fire able to start a much larger one.

rows.definition: Small points of light appearing and going. Sparkle is delight made visible and adds nothing functional, which is the point.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Delight that refuses to justify itself by being useful for anything else — the moment it starts doing a job, it has stopped being sparkle.
rows.historical_meaning: From spark (Old English spearca, a small fire), with the frequentative suffix -le; small points of light appearing and gone.

rows.definition: Belonging to space and position. Of what is understood by where things are relative to each other.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Belonging to space and position — understood by where things stand relative to one another rather than by any other measure.
rows.historical_meaning: From space (Latin spatium, an extent), with the suffix -al; understood by where things stand relative to one another.

rows.definition: Short form of specification — a statement of exactly what a thing must be. A spec is a contract before it is a plan.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A statement agreed before the building starts, so that disagreement about what a thing should be happens on paper rather than after the effort of making it is already spent.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin species (a kind, an appearance) + facere (to make), by way of specification; a statement of exactly what a thing must be, a contract before it is ever a plan.

rows.definition: Not of the general kind. Special cases are where general rules find out whether they were right.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Set apart from the general kind — and every special case is where a general rule finds out whether it was actually right.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin specialis (individual, particular), from species (a kind, an appearance), from specere (to look at, behold) — the same root as species; set apart from the general kind.
